title: The bottleneck rule: a system moves at the speed of its slowest part
story:
Effort goes where it is most visible, most interesting, or most familiar. A system's speed is set by none of those. It is set by one part, and an improvement anywhere else changes nothing you can measure.

Eliyahu Goldratt introduced the Theory of Constraints in The Goal, written with Jeff Cox and first published in 1984. Its premise is that every system has at least one constraint limiting its performance, and that a constraint is anything preventing the system from achieving its goal. The method is a cycle of five focusing steps: identify the constraint, exploit it, subordinate the other processes to it, elevate it, and repeat. Asked once to summarise the theory in a single sentence, Goldratt is reported to have offered a single word instead: focus.

Notice what the third step actually demands, because it is the one that meets resistance. Subordinating everything else to the constraint means deliberately running other parts below their capacity, which looks like waste and reads on a dashboard as underutilisation. It is neither. A part running faster than the constraint is producing work the constraint cannot absorb, and that work becomes queue rather than throughput.

The engineering version is arithmetic anybody can do and almost nobody does before starting. Suppose a request spends two milliseconds executing application code and a hundred and eighty milliseconds waiting on an unindexed database query. Rewriting the application in a faster language and cutting its two milliseconds to a fifth of that improves the total by less than one percent. Three months of work, invisible to every user. The index would have taken an afternoon.

The same result appears in computing in its own right, as Amdahl argued in 1967: the fraction of work that must be performed serially bounds the speedup available from any number of processors, so the maximum is the reciprocal of that fraction. Two fields, two vocabularies, one arithmetic — whatever you cannot improve sets the ceiling on everything you can.

The final step is the one that keeps it honest. Once the constraint is relieved, it moves. Index the query and the bottleneck becomes the application code, or the network, or connection acquisition. A system does not become fast; it becomes limited by something else, and the work is to find out what rather than to assume the previous answer still holds.

problem.name: The constraint
problem.shape: A system is too slow and effort is available to improve any part of it.
tell: an optimisation is chosen by what is interesting rather than by measurement
a rewrite produced no measurable change for users
utilisation is being maximised across every component
the bottleneck was identified once and never re-checked
problem.move: Measure to find the constraint before optimising anything, then work only on it. Accept that other parts will run below capacity, because output they produce beyond the constraint's rate becomes queue rather than throughput. When the constraint is relieved, find the new one rather than assuming the old answer holds.
problem.invariant: Improvement anywhere other than the constraint does not change the system's output, and the ceiling on total speedup is the reciprocal of the fraction you cannot improve.
problem.breaks: The constraint moves the moment it is relieved, so every answer has a shelf life. A team that optimises against last quarter's bottleneck is doing the same thing as a team that never measured — working somewhere other than the constraint — while believing itself disciplined.

cost.time: measurement before action, which delays visible progress and is the step under pressure to skip
cost.beats: optimising what is familiar, which is faster to start and changes nothing, and optimising everything, which spends effort in proportion to the number of parts rather than to their importance

worked.problem: A team spent three months rewriting a service in a faster language and users noticed nothing. Why?
worked.reasoning:
Because the part they rewrote was not the constraint, and improvement anywhere other than the constraint does not change the system's output.

The arithmetic settles it before any judgement is needed. Suppose a request spends two milliseconds in application code and a hundred and eighty milliseconds waiting on an unindexed database query. The rewrite attacks the two milliseconds. Even reducing it to nothing at all improves the total by roughly one percent — and a user cannot perceive that. The three months were spent on the part that was already fast.

The framing that predicts this is the Theory of Constraints: every system has at least one constraint limiting its performance, a constraint being anything that prevents the system from achieving its goal. The five focusing steps make the work sequential — identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, repeat — and the ordering is the content, because starting anywhere other than identify is how three months disappear. The one-word summary attributed to Goldratt is focus, and it is a claim about where effort goes rather than about effort's intensity.

The same result exists natively in computing. Amdahl's argument of 1967 is that the fraction which must be performed serially bounds the speedup from any number of processors, so the maximum is the reciprocal of that fraction. Ten percent serial means a ceiling of ten times however much hardware you buy. Two fields, two vocabularies, one arithmetic: whatever you cannot improve sets the ceiling on everything you can.

Why teams do this anyway is worth naming, because it is not stupidity. The application code is the part they own, understand and enjoy. The database index belongs to someone else, or to nobody, and finding it requires measurement rather than reasoning. The constraint is frequently the part of the system nobody wants to touch, which is part of why it became the constraint.

And the step that keeps this honest long-term is the last one. Once the constraint is relieved, it moves — index the query and the limit becomes the application code, or the network, or connection acquisition. So a bottleneck identified last quarter is not a bottleneck you still have. A team optimising against a stale answer is doing exactly what the undisciplined team does, working somewhere other than the constraint, while believing itself rigorous.

The uncomfortable implication I would state explicitly: subordinating other processes to the constraint means deliberately running parts of the system below their capacity. That reads as underutilisation on a dashboard and is correct, because output produced faster than the constraint can absorb becomes queue rather than throughput.

problem.practice: Take the last optimisation your team shipped and work out what fraction of total time it addressed. Then measure where the time actually goes on your slowest endpoint, and check whether the answer matches what anyone would have guessed.

beats.broke: Effort goes to whatever is most visible, interesting or familiar, and a system's speed is set by none of those — it is set by one part, and improving any other part changes nothing.
beats.fix: Find the constraint before optimising anything, then work only on it — identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, repeat — and expect it to move somewhere else once relieved.
beats.cost: Identifying the constraint requires measurement rather than reasoning, and the answer is frequently the part nobody on the team owns or enjoys working on.

interview.q: A team spent three months rewriting a service in a faster language and users noticed nothing. Why?
interview.trap: Concluding the rewrite was badly executed. It may have been excellent — it addressed a part that was already fast, and reducing two milliseconds inside a hundred and eighty-two changes the total by about one percent however well it is done.
